metadata.title: SponsorSQL: Plain-English Questions, Answers You Can Check
metadata.audience: INFO 7375 reviewers and Data Analyst hiring managers
metadata.persona: Atharva (first person; script written with Claude and reviewed by the author; synthetic Kokoro voice, disclosed in B12)
metadata.note: INFO 7375 Final Project demo, four parts in order: executive summary (B00-B01), introduction (B02), methods (B03-B07), evaluation (B08-B11), outro (B12). Every number on screen comes from saved output of the real system in fall-2026/atharva-h/final-project (evidence/ and evals/results/), re-typeset for legibility and labelled as such. The SQL proposals were real Claude replies from separate Claude Code subagents on 2026-11-21, replayed by the agent; no live CLI call is shown or claimed. No Claude chat response is shown. The human gate prompt is shown as the interactive prompt text; no owner decision is claimed.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Atharva. This is my final project, Sponsor S Q L. International students like me want to know which employers file H one B paperwork for jobs like ours. H one B is the main U.S. work visa for skilled jobs. That information is public, but it sits in one giant government spreadsheet that most students can't search.
beats.new_visual_element: A student's question next to a giant spreadsheet

shot.visual_intent: Part tag '1 · Executive summary'. Left: a big spreadsheet grid labelled 'DOL disclosure file · 437,496 filings'. Right: a question card. Caption defines H-1B.

show.event: part tag; caption 'H-1B: the main U.S. work visa for skilled jobs'
question card: 'Which employers file H-1Bs for Data Analysts?'

beats.narration_text: So Sponsor S Q L does one simple thing. You ask in plain English. It gives you the number, the S Q L query behind it, and the rows it counted, so you can check the answer, instead of just trusting it.
beats.new_visual_element: Hesitant writer: 'answers you can trust' corrected to 'answers you can check'

beats.narration_text: What already exists? Sites like My Visa Jobs and an H one B salary explorer let you search filings by employer and job title. A chatbot can write the query: when I asked Chat G P T about data analyst cases in Boston, it said forty, but nothing checked it. Sponsor S Q L adds two things: you see the query and the rows, and I publish how often it's wrong.
beats.new_visual_element: Three existing tools, then what SponsorSQL adds

shot.visual_intent: Part tag '2 · Introduction'. Three cards (MyVisaJobs, H-1B salary explorer, ChatGPT test) and a SponsorSQL card with two added features.

show.event: part tag; MyVisaJobs and salary-explorer cards
ChatGPT card: 'wrote a query · said 40 · nothing checked it'
SponsorSQL card: 'query + matching rows shown', 'error rate published', terracotta check

beats.narration_text: Now, how it works. The data is the Labor Department's latest file of Labor Condition Applications, the form an employer files before hiring someone on an H one B. The loader checks the file's fingerprint, drops five hundred ninety-five thousand blank rows, and keeps four hundred thirty-seven thousand real filings, with eighteen public columns. Contact names and emails are never loaded.
beats.new_visual_element: From the 252 MB workbook to a small database

shot.visual_intent: Part tag '3 · Methods'. Workbook page, checksum chip, row funnel (1,032,735 to 437,496), column funnel (98 to 18), crossed-out contact columns. Caption defines LCA.

show.event: part tag; workbook page 'FY2026 Q3 · 252 MB'; LCA caption

beats.narration_text: It's an agent, so it runs a loop. Observe the question. Decide whether to refuse it, then ask Claude for a query. Act: run it. Record every step. And stop: on a person's decision, a refusal, or a spent budget of two tries and ten seconds per query. Never just because the model says it's done.
beats.new_visual_element: The agent loop with its budget

shot.visual_intent: Five boxes in a ring (observe, decide, act, record, stop) lit in narration order; budget chips; caption defines agent.

show.event: part tag; caption 'Agent: software that repeats look, decide, act, record, stop'

chip 'not when the model says it's done'

beats.narration_text: The tool is a database query, guarded by a permission policy written in code. The database opens read-only, and a SQLite rule allows reading one table, nothing else. In this real output, a delete and a hidden second statement are refused, and the table still has every row.

shot.visual_intent: Left: read-only database with a rule chip. Right: dark terminal panel with real failure-case output lines (F1-F3) and rows before/after. Label 'real output, 2026-11-21, re-typeset'.

show.event: part tag; caption 'SQL query: instructions that pick and count rows'
database box 'read-only' and chip 'rule: only table lca'
terminal lines F1, F2, F3 type in

beats.narration_text: Here's a real run. The question: how many certified H one B data analyst cases are in Boston? The answer, forty, the S Q L, and the forty matching rows. Then the human gate: a person approves, refuses, or defers, and that decision is tied to a fingerprint of this exact screen.
beats.new_visual_element: Real run output and the human gate

beats.narration_text: What it needs: Python's standard library, SQLite, and my Claude Code account. No packages installed, no paid credits. The Claude command line wasn't logged in, so the queries tested here came from separate Claude sessions, saved word for word and replayed.

shot.visual_intent: Three resource chips and a note box about recorded replies. Caption defines Claude Code.

show.event: part tag; caption 'Claude Code: Anthropic's AI coding assistant'
chips: Python standard library + SQLite; Claude Code account; no paid credits
note: 'CLI: Not logged in → replies from separate Claude sessions, saved and replayed'

beats.narration_text: How do I know it works? Before any test, two question sets were frozen: ten for development and five held out, with answer keys counted by separate code that never sees the model's query. The bar: eight out of ten, four out of five, and no unsafe query.
beats.new_visual_element: Frozen question sets, answer keys and the pass bar

shot.visual_intent: Part tag '4 · Evaluation'. Two locked boxes (10 development, 5 held-out) each with an answer key; three bar chips. Caption defines answer key.

show.event: part tag; caption 'Answer key: the right answers, counted separately'

beats.narration_text: First try: four out of ten. It matched job titles too loosely, so Metadata Analyst counted as a data analyst. A title-matching rule fixed that: nine out of ten. The one miss came from invisible tab characters in four job titles. Then the held-out set, scored once: five out of five.

shot.visual_intent: Three bars grow on the spoken numbers with short notes under each. Caption defines held-out.

show.event: part tag; caption 'Held-out: questions kept aside and scored only once'
bar 9/10 with note 'miss: tab characters in 4 titles'

beats.narration_text: I also tried to break it on purpose. Ten deliberate failures, unsafe queries, a runaway query, questions about contact details or visa chances, and a stale approval, were all stopped as predicted. The original title bug, triggered on purpose, was caught by the answer key.
beats.new_visual_element: Ten deliberate failure cases and the controlled failure

shot.visual_intent: A 2x5 grid of tiles (F1-F10) each getting a check, then a wide tile for the controlled failure. Label: scripted test inputs, not model output.

show.event: part tag; label 'scripted test inputs, not model output'
tiles F1-F10 appear and get checks
wide tile 'title bug triggered on purpose → caught by the answer key'

beats.narration_text: An independent reviewer found eighteen problems, and the ones code could fix were fixed. Three limits remain. The final rules were scored before I reviewed them. The answer keys share their rules with the system. And the replies were replayed, not live. So the honest claim is narrow: one public file, answers you can check. Ship, narrow, or defer is my sign-off, still open.
